meta.title: Quality and time as competitive tools
meta.summary: Design and conformance quality, the four costs of quality, tools for finding quality problems, relevant costs of quality decisions, customer-response time and queues, and the theory of constraints.

videos.title: Two kinds of quality
videos.take: Quality of design fits the product to customer needs; conformance quality makes it to specification

scenes.say: For a differentiator like Tallgrass, quality isn't optional. But quality means two different things.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of quality
scenes.say: Quality of design is how well a product's features match what customers need: a fifty-mile range when commuters need seventy is a design failure. Conformance quality is how well the product meets its own specifications: a motor seal that leaks is a conformance failure.

sub: conformance failures create rework and claims
scenes.say: Both cost money. Design failures lose sales to better-designed rivals. Conformance failures create rework, warranty claims and angry customers.
Many companies certify their processes under the ISO nine thousand standards, which require documented, consistent quality procedures. Some large buyers insist on it.
Quality measures sit in the internal-process perspective of the balanced scorecard from Lecture 10, and drive customer satisfaction and financial results.

scenes.q: Tallgrass's bikes meet every specification, but buyers want a longer range than the design offers. This is a failure of:
scenes.say: Quick check. Tallgrass's bikes meet every specification, but buyers want more range than the design offers. What's failing? Pause and pick.

videos.title: The costs of quality
videos.take: Costs of quality fall into prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure

scenes.say: Poor quality is expensive, but the costs are scattered across the company. A cost-of-quality report pulls them together.

scenes.heading: Four categories
scenes.say: Prevention costs stop defects from happening: design reviews, supplier evaluation, training. Appraisal costs find defects before shipping: inspection and testing. Internal failure costs arise from defects caught in-house: rework and scrap. External failure costs arise after the sale: warranty repairs, returns and lost future sales.

scenes.heading: Tallgrass cost-of-quality report, 2027
scenes.say: Tallgrass's 2027 report: $60,000 of prevention, $70,000 of appraisal, $60,000 of internal failure and $180,000 of external failure, including an estimated $70,000 of contribution from lost sales. Total: $370,000, almost thirteen percent of revenue.

sub: A dollar spent preventing defects saves
scenes.say: The pattern is typical: most of the cost is failure, especially external failure. Shifting spending toward prevention usually lowers the total.

sub: Lost sales aren't in the ledger,
scenes.say: Notice that lost sales are an opportunity cost, estimated, not recorded in the accounts. Ignoring them understates how much poor quality really costs.

scenes.q: Road-testing every finished bike is which category?
scenes.say: Quick check. Road-testing every finished bike is which category? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, appraisal: finding defects before shipping.

videos.title: Finding quality problems
videos.take: Control charts spot problems, Pareto diagrams rank them, and fishbone diagrams trace their causes

scenes.say: To fix quality problems you have to find them, rank them, and trace their causes. Three tools help.

sub: Plots a process over time against
scenes.say: A control chart plots a process measure, like defects per day, against limits set from its normal variation, often two or three standard deviations from the mean. Points outside the limits signal a problem to investigate.

scenes.heading: Pareto: warranty claims by cause, 2027
scenes.say: A Pareto diagram ranks problems by frequency. Of eighty-two warranty claims, forty-one were motor seal leaks and twenty-two battery connector faults. Two causes account for three-quarters of claims. Fix those first.

scenes.heading: Fishbone: why do seals leak?
items: Methods: seal pressed at an angle
scenes.say: A cause-and-effect, or fishbone, diagram lists possible causes under headings like methods, machines, materials and people. For the leaking seals: a seal pressed at an angle, a worn press fixture, a supplier's new rubber compound, or untrained new assemblers.
Then the team tests the candidate causes with data. At Tallgrass, leaks clustered in bikes built after the supplier changed its rubber compound.

scenes.q: Which tool ranks problems by how often they occur?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which tool ranks problems by frequency? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Is a quality improvement worth it?
videos.take: Compare the relevant costs of a quality program with the failure costs it saves, including lost contribution

scenes.say: A better motor seal costs more. Is it worth it? Relevant cost analysis answers.

scenes.heading: Upgraded seal: costs
scenes.say: The upgraded seal costs an extra twenty-five dollars a bike, $30,000 for twelve hundred bikes, plus $15,000 of one-time redesign and testing: $45,000.

scenes.heading: Upgraded seal: savings
scenes.say: It's expected to avoid $40,000 of warranty repairs and $10,000 of rework, and to recover twenty lost sales worth $900 each in contribution, $18,000. Savings total $68,000, a net benefit of $23,000.
Include only costs that actually change. If Tallgrass keeps its inspectors anyway, their salaries aren't savings, even if they inspect fewer seals.
And count the nonfinancial benefits: brand reputation, dealer confidence and fewer riders stranded with a dead motor, which matter a great deal for a differentiator.

scenes.q: A $50,000 program saves $30,000 of warranty costs and recovers 25 sales at $900 CM. Net benefit?
scenes.say: Quick check. A fifty thousand dollar program saves thirty thousand of warranty costs and recovers twenty-five sales at nine hundred dollars contribution. Net benefit? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Customer-response time and queues
videos.take: Response time includes waiting; as capacity fills, waiting time grows sharply

scenes.say: Customers care how fast they get their bike. Most of the delay isn't work; it's waiting.

scenes.heading: Customer-response time
scenes.say: Customer-response time runs from the order to delivery. It includes receipt time, until the order reaches production; waiting time in the queue; manufacturing time; and delivery time.
For a single bottleneck with random order arrivals, average waiting time can be estimated as orders times processing time squared, divided by two times the capacity left over.

scenes.heading: Custom paint booth: 4,000 hours a year
scenes.say: Tallgrass's custom paint booth has four thousand hours a year. A hundred orders at thirty hours each means an average wait of forty-five hours. Add twenty-five new orders at twenty hours, and the booth is eighty-seven and a half percent busy: the average wait more than doubles to a hundred hours.

The lesson: waiting time rises steeply as a resource approaches full use. A new product can slow every existing order. The cost of those delays, lost sales and price discounts, belongs in the decision.

scenes.q: Orders 50 × 40 hours; capacity 3,000 hours. Average waiting time?
scenes.say: Quick check. Fifty orders at forty hours each; capacity three thousand hours. Average waiting time? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's A. 50 times 1,600 is 80,000, divided by 2 times 1,000 spare hours: forty hours.

videos.title: The theory of constraints
videos.take: Manage the bottleneck: maximize throughput margin through it, then relieve it

scenes.say: The theory of constraints says one resource limits the whole system. Manage that, and the rest follows.
The theory of constraints focuses on throughput margin: revenue minus direct materials. In the short run, other costs are treated as fixed.

scenes.heading: Five steps
scenes.say: Five steps: identify the bottleneck; get the most throughput margin out of it; pace everything else to it, avoiding inventory piling up in front; relieve the bottleneck by adding capacity; then find the next one.

scenes.heading: Relieving the paint booth
items: Never let it sit idle: cover breaks
Shift simple jobs to an outside painter
Add a second booth if margin justifies it
scenes.say: For the paint booth: never let it sit idle, covering breaks; inspect frames before painting so the booth never paints a defective frame; send simple jobs to an outside painter; and add a second booth if the extra throughput margin justifies the cost.

scenes.big: An hour lost at the bottleneck
sub: is an hour lost for the whole plant
scenes.say: The key insight: an hour lost at the bottleneck is an hour lost for the whole plant, while an hour saved elsewhere is often worth nothing.

scenes.q: Where should quality inspection happen if painting is the bottleneck?
scenes.say: Quick check. If painting is the bottleneck, where should inspection happen? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, before painting, so the bottleneck never wastes time on defective frames.

The booth now handles 100 orders at 30 hours (4,000-hour capacity). Without: 45 hours; with: 100 hours (+55 → about 11 lost orders × $1,400 = $15,400). New line margin 25 × 600 = $15,000. Roughly break-even or worse: don't add unless the booth is relieved, by inspecting before painting, outsourcing simple jobs, or adding capacity.
